problem: DRL visual navigation was validated only in simulation, relying on simulator-provided signals (segmentation masks, distance to goal, stop signal from the simulator) that are unavailable on a real robot, so learned policies cannot be deployed directly.
motivation: End-to-end DRL policies are cheap to run, map-free and need only a camera, but sim-only assumptions block real deployment. The paper removes those privileged signals so the policy can run with just an RGB camera and a goal image, and bridges the sim-to-real gap via pre-training plus fine-tuning on real images.
key_idea: Replace privileged auxiliary tasks (segmentation) with raw-image reconstruction tasks and add a learned terminate action, pre-train in a fast Quake III/DeepMind Lab office simulator, then fine-tune on a grid of real-world images so the policy runs on a real robot with only RGB and a goal image.
insight: Image-reconstruction auxiliary tasks sharing the latent space with actor and critic speed and stabilize learning without labels: in the simulator the method reaches 1.000 success against 0.420 for PAAC and 0.999 for UNREAL. Simulator pre-training gives a clear gain on the real dataset (0.936 vs 0.883 for 'np ours', and similar gains for PAAC and UNREAL). A learned terminate action removes the need for a localization module at test time.
method: Network: CNN base + LSTM (512) + actor/critic heads, taking the current image, goal image, previous action and reward as inputs; trained with PAAC with off-policy critic updates.

Auxiliary tasks: pixel control, reward prediction, depth reconstruction, plus new reconstruction of the observation image and the target image (replacing segmentation masks) to shape the conv features without labels.

Terminate action: the agent decides when to stop; reward +1 if it stops at the goal, -0.1 if it stops near a wrong-type object in simulation, and a negative reward if the step limit is hit; no simulator stop signal is needed.

Environment simulator: DeepMind Lab / Quake III Arena with procedurally generated office rooms (random bookshelves, chairs, cabinets along walls); the target image is taken near a chosen target object; the layout is kept for 50 episodes.

Real-world fine-tuning: a TurtleBot 2 with RGB-D collects images at grid points (0.2 m resolution) in 4 directions with odometry poses; the agent is fine-tuned on-policy by rolling out on this image grid with curriculum learning.
Deployment: only the RGB camera and the goal image are needed at test time (no depth, no localization); success means within 0.3 m and 30° of the goal.

setting.backbone: CNN (4 conv layers) + LSTM actor-critic trained with PAAC + auxiliary tasks, trained from scratch
setting.training_data: 8M frames in the custom DeepMind Lab office simulator (pre-training), then 30M frames of on-policy rollouts on a real-world image grid dataset collected in one office (0.2 m grid, 4 headings)
setting.observation: monocular RGB (84x84) plus goal image; the previous action and reward are also fed in
setting.action_space: discrete grid moves (forward, 90° turns) plus a learned terminate action
setting.simulator: custom DeepMind Lab / Quake III Arena office simulator plus a real-image grid dataset
setting.privileged: none at test time (depth and odometry poses are used only during dataset collection and fine-tuning; odometry is used only to evaluate success)

results: In simulation the method reaches a 100% success rate versus 42.0% for PAAC and 99.9% for UNREAL, with slightly shorter paths than UNREAL. On the real image dataset it gets 93.6% (PAAC 92.2%, UNREAL 86.3%), and on a real TurtleBot it succeeds in 26 of 30 trials (86.7%) with 0.175 m mean goal distance.
limitations: The evaluation is small (30 real trials) and restricted to a single office with grid-constrained motion and discrete 90° turns; fine-tuning needs robot pose data with the images.
Success is judged by noisy odometry with a lenient 0.3 m / 30° tolerance.
The agent has limited memory (LSTM) and is not tested in larger environments or with continuous actions.
